name: Collimated beam
description: The collimator again, for a real beam: 16 particles leave the source with a spread of directions (σ = 4°) and repel each other on the way. At least 90 % must reach the detector travelling parallel to the axis (within ±3°). Only charges of the particle's sign are available.

remarks.detail: The particles repel each other with the exact Coulomb force (with c = ∞ that is the whole interaction), so an intense beam spreads as a real one does.

remarks.line: A beam of a few particles
remarks.detail: A dozen or so particles stand for a beam of billions: each carries the charge of many (its mass and energy scaled alike, so that its own path is unchanged), so their repulsion matches an intense beam's. The spreads are a fixed sample of the beam's distribution, the same every time.
Real ion optics use shaped electrodes with small aberrations; a few point charges make lenses and deflectors with large ones, which the detectors' tolerances absorb.

Everything is symmetric about the plane z = 0, so the particle never leaves it. A real beam also has a width across the plane, where the same fields act differently (focusing in the plane can defocus across it).
